<h1 align="center">camtrapReport</h1>

<p align="center">
  <em>Reproducible reporting for camera-trap monitoring data</em>
</p>

---

`camtrapReport` converts camera-trap data in
[Camtrap DP](https://camtrap-dp.tdwg.org/) format into two coordinated HTML
outputs:

- a **Data Status Check**, which identifies issues in data completeness,
  consistency, annotation, and spatiotemporal coverage; and
- an **Ecological Report**, which combines selected ecological summaries,
  analyses, figures, tables, maps, metadata, and explanatory text in a
  configurable report.

Shiny supports the optional `gui()` interface. The code-based workflow does
not start a Shiny application.

The package focuses on the reporting workflow. It complements tools for
camera-trap data management and specialised ecological modelling rather than
replacing them.

<p align="center">
  <img src="vignettes/figures/package-architecture.png"
       width="900"
       alt="Workflow from Camtrap DP input through camtrapReport to the Data Status Check and Ecological Report">
  <br>
  <em>Workflow from Camtrap DP input through camtrapReport to the Data Status Check and Ecological Report.</em>
</p>

Follow the diagram with the [Data Status Check guide](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/data-status-report.html),
[Ecological Report guide](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/ecological-report.html),
[module editing guide](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/modules.html),
and [reusable profiles guide](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/profiles.html).
The last two explain how to customise the analyses and narrative text.

### Bundled analyses

The `default` profile selects the following ecological modules. Availability
of a module does not establish that its method is suitable for a dataset;
some need optional packages, habitat information, or additional measurements.

| Report component | Module names | Main requirements or interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Context and methods | `introduction`, `methods`, `study_area`, `sampling`, `location`, `effort`, `image_processing`, `data_processing` | Metadata, deployment information, and optional study-area boundary. |
| Captures and trends | `results`, `captures`, `abundance_trends` | Observation and effort summaries; capture rates are not density estimates. |
| Random encounter model (REM) | `population_density`, `model_parameters`, `population_densities` | Species-specific detection, speed, activity, and effort data; the default pools fitted parameters across years. |
| Activity and community summaries | `activity_patterns`, `richness`, `co_occurrence`, `species_accumulation` | Timestamps, species identities, and adequate observations for each method. |
| Spatial and habitat summaries | `spatial_density`, `habitat_preferences` | Camera coordinates and, for habitat comparisons, habitat input. |
| Supporting sections | `acknowledgements`, `appendix`, `References` | Narrative, supplementary outputs, and citations; the default appendix is HTML-only. |

The status profile contains `abstract`, `spatial`, `temporal`, `availability`,
`validation`, `annotation`, `observation_type`, `conclusion`, and `acknowledge`.
The `EOW` profile selects customised alternatives, including annual REM
parameters. Inspect the exact selections with
`section_names(profile = "default")` or `section_names(profile = "EOW")`.

### Preparing data from another format

`camData()` reads an existing Camtrap DP directory or ZIP archive; it does not
convert arbitrary camera-trap tables. If your platform supports Camtrap DP
export, use that export (for example, Agouti and TRAPPER are listed by the
[Camtrap DP standard](https://camtrap-dp.tdwg.org/#software)). Otherwise, map
your fields and identifiers to the standard's linked tables and metadata.
The [camtrapdp package](https://inbo.github.io/camtrapdp/reference/index.html)
can read, edit, and write existing Camtrap DP objects; its writer is not a
general converter from arbitrary input tables.

The checks in `camtrapReport` assess reporting readiness; they are not full
Camtrap DP schema validation. For schema validation, follow the
[standard's Frictionless validation instructions](https://camtrap-dp.tdwg.org/#validation).
`camtrapdp::check_camtrapdp()` checks a Camtrap DP R object's required
properties and serves a different purpose.

## Use in practice

Although `camtrapReport` has not yet been applied in a published ecological study, it has been developed and evaluated using real-world camera-trap monitoring datasets from multiple study sites across North America, Asia, Europe, Africa, and Australia. Evaluation involved both developer-led testing and independent users who applied the package to their own datasets and provided feedback. In Europe, this evaluation has drawn particularly on datasets available through camera-trap research networks, including the [European Observatory of Wildlife network](https://enetwild.com/), which spans diverse geographic settings and monitoring designs.

Experience across these heterogeneous datasets has informed checks for metadata completeness and spatiotemporal coverage, improvements to report generation, and revisions based on user feedback. Related publications, presentations, and training activities are listed on the [Resources page](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/resources.html).


## Installation

`camtrapReport` requires R 4.1.0 or later. Install it from GitHub with
[`pak`](https://pak.r-lib.org/):

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("pak", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pak")
}

pak::pkg_install(
  "spatialecology/camtrapReport"
)
```

To automatically check and install packages required by available, newly added, or updated report modules:

```{r module-dependencies, eval=FALSE}
camtrapReport::install_all()
```

`install_all()` scans the bundled and registered user modules and installs any
missing dependencies when you explicitly call it. It is not needed for the
small report below. Before installing the optional analysis stack, inspect
the `#| packages:` declarations in the YAML modules you intend to run; the
[module guide](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/modules.html#inspect-dependencies-without-installing)
shows how to inspect these declarations without installing packages.

## Quick start

This executed example uses a compact Camtrap DP dataset derived from
**GMU8_LEUVEN**, together with bundled habitat data and a study-area boundary.
The dataset is copied to a temporary directory because `camData()` may store
processed files beside writable input data.

```{r quick-start}
library(camtrapReport)

example_root <- tempfile("camtrapReport-example-")

dir.create(
  example_root,
  recursive = TRUE
)

copied <- file.copy(
  from = system.file(
    "external",
    "dataset",
    package = "camtrapReport",
    mustWork = TRUE
  ),
  to = example_root,
  recursive = TRUE,
  copy.mode = FALSE
)

habitat <- utils::read.csv(
  system.file(
    "external",
    "habitat",
    "habitat.csv",
    package = "camtrapReport",
    mustWork = TRUE
  )
)

study_area <- system.file(
  "external",
  "study_area",
  "study_area.shp",
  package = "camtrapReport",
  mustWork = TRUE
)
```

```{r validate-example-data, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(copied),
  dir.exists(file.path(example_root, "dataset"))
)
```

```{r create-camreport-object, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
cm <- camData(
  data = file.path(example_root, "dataset"),
  habitat = habitat,
  study_area = study_area,
  update = TRUE
)
```

```{r show-camreport-object}
cm
```

`camData()` also accepts a Camtrap DP ZIP archive or an extracted Camtrap DP
directory. Habitat data and a study-area boundary are optional.

`camData()` saves `__camReport_Object.rds` in the extracted dataset directory.
When a study-area boundary is supplied, it also saves `study_area.map` there.
Keep these files with the dataset if you want to reuse the processed object.
After correcting source CSV/JSON files, reload with `update = TRUE` to rebuild
the cached object before generating another report.

To make the quick start small and reproducible without optional analysis
packages, use an introduction-only ecological report and three status modules:

```{r quick-start-profile}
quick_start <- reportProfile(
  name = "quick-start",
  report = "introduction",
  status = c("spatial", "temporal", "availability")
)
```

### Generate a Data Status Check
`status()` generates a Data Status Check report that provides a structured
assessment of whether the camera-trap dataset is ready for ecological reporting.
It summarises five core areas: spatial quality, temporal coverage, essential data
availability, classification and validation, and annotation quality. The report
also summarises observation types by capture method and highlights issues that
require attention. Review the measured check tables and their warnings to
decide what should be corrected before ecological analysis. There is no
computed overall quality grade or automatic gate preventing `report()` from
running. The function returns the path to the
generated report; set `view = TRUE` to open it.



```{r generate-data-status, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
status_file <- status(
  cm,
  profile = quick_start,
  filename = file.path(example_root, "quick-start-status.html"),
  view = FALSE
)
```

[**View Data Status Check output**](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/reports/DataStatusReport_example.html)

The linked report illustrates a full status report, rather than the three
modules selected in this quick start. After correcting issues in your source
data, repeat `cm <- camData(data_path, update = TRUE)` and `status(cm, ...)`.
`status()` diagnoses issues; it does not repair source records.

```{r validate-data-status, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  is.character(status_file),
  length(status_file) == 1L,
  file.exists(status_file)
)
```

### Generate an Ecological Report
`report()` generates a structured Ecological Report that brings together the
selected analytical modules in a single, reproducible document. Depending on the
available data and selected report sections, it can include information on
sampling effort, species richness and occurrence, co-occurrence, activity
patterns, habitat use, abundance and density, species accumulation, and spatial
patterns. Analytical results are integrated with tables, figures, maps, and
automatically generated narrative text that adapts to the underlying data and
metadata, providing an interpretable overview of the camera-trap monitoring
dataset. Because the report is modular, users can select, omit, reorder, or
extend sections according to their data and reporting needs. The function
returns the path to the generated report; set `view = TRUE` to open it.

```{r generate-ecological-report, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
report_file <- report(
  cm,
  profile = quick_start,
  filename = file.path(example_root, "quick-start-report.html"),
  view = FALSE
)
```

[**View Ecological Report output**](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/reports/EcologicalReport_example.html)

The linked report is a separate, more complete illustration. Its data,
profile, optional inputs, and selected analyses may differ from this quick
start. To request the bundled standard or EOW selection explicitly, use
`report(cm, profile = "default", filename = ...)` or
`report(cm, profile = "EOW", filename = ...)` after reviewing module
requirements. `test = TRUE` tests modules and excludes failing ones; a report
produced that way can therefore contain fewer sections. It is a diagnostic
tool, not a way to make missing analyses equivalent to successful ones.

```{r validate-ecological-report, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  is.character(report_file),
  length(report_file) == 1L,
  file.exists(report_file)
)
```

## Configure a report

Inspect report metadata and choose which sections to include:

```{r configure-report, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
info(
  cm,
  name = c("title", "authors")
)

section_names()

selected_sections <- section_names(
  keep = c(
    "introduction",
    "methods",
    "study_area",
    "sampling",
    "effort"
  )
)

sections(
  cm,
  selected_sections
)
```

Named profiles provide reusable module selections. Bundled profiles can be
listed and inspected without changing the module pool:

```{r report-profiles, eval=FALSE}
profile_names(cm)
section_names(object = cm, profile = "EOW")

# Select and render the EOW profile
report(
  cm,
  profile = "EOW",
  filename = file.path(tempdir(), "EOW-report.html")
)

# Profiles can be shared independently of module YAML files
write_profile(
  "EOW",
  file.path(tempdir(), "EOW-profile.yml"),
  object = cm
)
```

HTML is the default output. To create a static PDF of the HTML-based report,
install the optional `pagedown` package and use either a PDF filename or
`format = "pdf"`. A supported Chrome or Edge browser is also required. PDF
reports omit the table of contents. Module compatibility is recorded as
`html`, `pdf`, or `both` in the `formats` column returned by
`list_Modules(tree = FALSE)`; incompatible modules are skipped for the selected
output format. Printable tabsets are expanded so all of their panels remain
visible in PDF output.

```{r pdf-output, eval=FALSE}
report(cm, filename = file.path(tempdir(), "ecological-report.pdf"))
status(cm, filename = file.path(tempdir(), "data-status.pdf"))
```

Reports can also be configured by taxonomic group, survey year, and
observation-count threshold. See the
[Ecological Report](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/ecological-report.html)
and
[Module management](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/modules.html)
guides for further examples.

Use `gui(cm)` to configure and generate reports through an interactive
interface.

Report narrative comes from the selected YAML modules' `text` fields and
their R code, together with metadata and text stored in `cm`. You can edit
the current object's text with `updateReportSection()` or `info()`, or copy
the module registry to a writable project directory and edit its YAML files
for reuse. A profile selects modules; it does not create their narrative or
analyses. See the [module editing guide](https://spatialecology.github.io/camtrapReport/articles/modules.html#editing-existing-modules)
for the copy, edit, reload, and test workflow. Only load modules from trusted
sources: module code and expressions embedded in text execute with your R
session's permissions.

### REM parameter scope

The standard profile uses the pooled REM modules: one set of detection,
movement-speed, and activity parameters is fitted per species across all
sampling years, while trap rate remains year-specific. The `EOW` profile uses
the annual REM module, which fits all parameters independently for every
species and sampling year:

```r
report(
  cm,
  profile = "EOW",
  filename = file.path(tempdir(), "EOW-annual-report.html")
)
```

Both methods remain available as report modules. The annual parent module is
`population_density_annual`; the pooled parent module is
`population_density`. REM output records the parameter scope, individual-count
unit, number of repetitions, and random seed used for the calculation.

### Map backgrounds

Report maps use a self-contained offline background by default. It does not
request web tiles, so saved reports remain readable without an internet
connection or a third-party tile service. A remote background can be requested
when internet access is available:

```r
cm$setting$map_basemap <- "openstreetmap" # OpenTopoMap fallback on tile failure
cm$setting$map_basemap <- "cartodb"       # or "esri"
cm$setting$map_basemap <- "offline"       # reproducible default
```

In OpenStreetMap mode, OpenTopoMap is placed underneath the primary tiles.
Successfully loaded OpenStreetMap tiles remain visible; failed tiles are
transparent so the fallback is revealed. Both services require internet
access. Use `"offline"` for archival and reproducible reports.

## Interpretation and reproducibility

A successful Data Status Check confirms that the implemented data checks were
completed; it does not establish that the survey design or data are suitable
for a particular ecological analysis. Results should be interpreted in
relation to sampling effort, detectability, season, habitat, and
method-specific assumptions.

For reproducibility, retain the input data, optional inputs, analytical
settings, selected report sections, and relevant package versions. General
guidance is available from the
[Reproducible Research CRAN Task View](https://cran.r-project.org/view=ReproducibleResearch).

Reports may contain maps or derived results that reveal sensitive species
locations. Review all content before sharing a report.

## Example-data provenance

The bundled example dataset is derived from the
[GMU8_LEUVEN Camtrap DP dataset](https://doi.org/10.15468/4u3wm4), published by
the Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO) through GBIF. It contains
8 derived location identifiers, 87 deployments, 15,492 retained media records,
and 11,092 observation records. The relationship-preserving subset is intended
for demonstration and software testing, not ecological inference. Its
preparation and media-reduction rules are documented in the
[example-data README](https://github.com/spatialecology/camtrapReport/blob/main/inst/external/README-Leuven-dataset.md).

## Relationship to other camera-trap packages

Several R packages support related parts of camera-trap workflows:

- [`camtrapdp`](https://inbo.github.io/camtrapdp/) reads, validates, and
  transforms Camtrap DP datasets;
- [`camtraptor`](https://inbo.github.io/camtraptor/) supports exploration and
  visualisation; and
- [`camtrapR`](https://jniedballa.github.io/camtrapR/) and
  [`ct`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ct) provide broader data-management
  and analysis workflows.

`camtrapReport` complements these packages by integrating data-status checks,
selected ecological analyses, figures, maps, tables, metadata, and explanatory
text within a configurable reporting workflow. Its extensible module framework
allows users to incorporate additional analyses and report components without
modifying the core package. To my knowledge, it is the first R package
designed specifically to automate the generation of both data-status and
ecological reports from camera-trap data.
